title: Red or rough, what makes materials warmer?
research_question: To what extent do surface roughness and material color influence the experience of material warmth, and how do these effects relate to each other?

participants.description: Pre-study: 20 (12 male) Architectural Engineering students, Vrije Universiteit Brussel, ages 17-22 (avg 18). Main study: 38 (71% female) Architecture students, Vrije Universiteit Brussel, ages 18-24 (avg 21). Total N=58 unique participants across both studies.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Inorganic Phosphate Cement (IPC) material samples, 20x20 cm. Pre-study Set I: 10 samples with different colors (Pure white, Light gray, Deep black, Chocolate brown, Ruby red, Mango yellow, Ivory beige, White green, Ice blue, Sapphire blue), semi-mat, even surface. Pre-study Set II: 10 samples with varying surface roughness (R01-R10), semi-mat light gray paint. Main study Set A: 4 samples (smooth/rough x light gray/mango yellow). Main study Set B: 4 samples (smooth/rough x ice blue/sapphire blue).

findings.mechanism: Color hue, lightness, and saturation contribute to warmth perception.
findings.quote: The repeated measures ANOVA shows a significant main effect of Color [F(5,88) = 20.4; p < 0.001; η² = 0.517].

findings.mechanism: Combination of hue, lightness, and saturation for reddish color adds to warm perception.
findings.quote: The mean perceived warmth of the Ruby red sample differs significantly (p < 0.001) from all other color samples, except the Mango yellow one.

findings.mechanism: Warm colors (yellowish (+b*) and reddish (+a*) hues) are perceived as warmer.
findings.quote: Ruby red and Mango yellow are perceived as the warmest colors from the set

findings.mechanism: Cool colors (bluish (-b*) and greenish (-a*) hues) are perceived as colder.
findings.quote: Light gray and Ice blue are the coldest colors

findings.mechanism: Darker colors tend to be perceived as warmer, and lighter colors as colder.
findings.quote: moderate negative correlation is found between perceived warmth and lightness L* (Pearson's r = -0.48).

findings.mechanism: The effect approached significance, suggesting a trend that needs further investigation.
findings.quote: No significant effect of Roughness is found in the repeated measures ANOVA [F(5,92) = 2.0; p = 0.09; η² = 0.095].

findings.mechanism: For flat materials, increasing local roughness leads to an increasing perception of warmth.
findings.quote: A visual representation of the means (Fig. 5) suggests that, for flat materials (R01-R05), an increasing local roughness leads to an increasing perception of warmth.

findings.antecedent: Material color (light gray, mango yellow, ice blue, sapphire blue)
findings.mechanism: Warmer colors (mango yellow and sapphire blue) lead to warmer overall perception than colder colors (light gray and ice blue).
findings.quote: shows significant main effects of both Color [F(3,101) = 54.3; p < 0.001; η² = 0.595]

findings.quote: The absence of a significant interaction effect Color × Roughness [F(3,103) = 0.4; p > 0.5] illustrates that the effect of roughness on material warmth is independent of the material's color and vice versa.

findings.quote: The effect of Roughness just failed to reach significance at the 0.05 level [F(1,37) = 3.8; p = 0.06; η² = 0.093].

findings.mechanism: The difference in warmth perception between light gray (mean 2.72) and sapphire blue (mean 3.67) is 0.95.
findings.quote: The difference in warmth perception between the light gray (mean 2.72) and the sapphire blue samples (mean 3.67) is 0.95.

findings.mechanism: The difference in warmth perception between smooth (mean 2.92) and rough (mean 3.47) samples is 0.55.
findings.quote: The difference in warmth perception between the smooth samples (mean 2.92) and the rough samples (mean 3.47) is 0.55.

findings.mechanism: The effect of color on the perception of material warmth is 1.7 times larger than the effect of increasing local roughness.
findings.quote: Relatively speaking, the effect of color on the perception of material warmth thus is 1.7 times larger than the effect of increasing the local roughness of a surface.

mechanisms: Color hue, saturation, and lightness contribute to the overall perception of warmth, with warmer hues (yellowish, reddish) leading to higher warmth ratings.
Local surface roughness contributes to the perception of warmth, with rougher surfaces being perceived as warmer than smooth surfaces.
The effects of color and roughness on warmth perception are mutually independent and can be summed when combined.
implementation_implications: Architects and designers can manipulate the intended warmth of a space or building through material color and surface roughness.
Color adjustments are more effective than surface roughness adjustments for changing perceived warmth of walls.
If radical color change is not desirable or possible, surface texture manipulation (e.g., different finishing techniques) can still alter warmth perception.
Materials with a rough surface and cold color will generally be perceived as colder than materials with a smooth surface and warm color.

tables.description: Qualitative descriptions, technical measurements (L*, a*, b*, I*), and mean warmth ratings for 10 color samples (Set I).
key_stats: Mean warmth ratings range from 2.45 (Ice blue, Light gray) to 6.30 (Ruby red).
L* values range from 28.79 (Deep black) to 94.80 (Pure white).
a* values range from -14.58 (White green) to 32.80 (Ruby red).
b* values range from -17.03 (Ice blue) to 74.02 (Mango yellow).

tables.description: Qualitative descriptions (material science and architecture) and mean warmth ratings for 10 roughness samples (Set II).
key_stats: Mean warmth ratings range from 2.95 (R06) to 4.15 (R05).
R01 (Flat - no local roughness) mean warmth = 3.00.
R05 (Flat - highest local roughness) mean warmth = 4.15.

tables.description: Overview of the eight samples created for the main study, based on pre-study results, combining specific colors and roughness levels.

limitations: The pre-study's finding on color lightness (L*) and warmth correlation should be considered with care due to the limited number of achromatic samples.

The study's findings on roughness might contain both visual and tactile components, and it is unclear which contributed more to the warmth perception. The effect of roughness might gain importance in applications where users frequently touch materials.
Material perception is context-dependent, and the results should be considered within the context of indoor wall applications.
The study did not investigate how the effects of color and roughness relate to a material's thermal properties.
The study did not investigate warmth perception for other materials (e.g., metal, wood) or for new/unknown materials compared to known ones.
